title: Preface
summary: Apple Inc.’s Form 10-K cover page identifies its annual report for the fiscal year ended September 24, 2022, its California incorporation, headquarters, contact details, and SEC file number. It lists common stock and debt securities registered on Nasdaq, with no Section 12(g) securities. The company reports its filer status, compliance with periodic and interactive-data filing requirements, internal-control attestation, and non-shell status. It also reports approximately $2.83 trillion in nonaffiliate market value as of March 25, 2022, and 15,908,118,000 shares outstanding as of October 14, 2022.

title: DOCUMENTS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
summary: Apple’s 2022 Form 10-K incorporates portions of its 2023 annual-meeting proxy statement into Part III and outlines the report’s four parts and items. It explains forward-looking statements, their risks, identifying terms, and no-update policy, and defines fiscal-year references and “Company”/“Apple.” Part I describes Apple’s business and fiscal calendar, then lists its iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Wearables, Home and Accessories product lines, including named devices, operating systems, and related accessories and services.

title: Apple Company Background and Products
summary: The page explains that Apple’s 10-K contains uncertain forward-looking statements, identifies their sources and wording, warns actual results may differ, cites risk factors, and disclaims an update obligation except as required by law. It defines fiscal-period references and “Company”/“Apple.” Apple designs, manufactures, and markets devices and services; its fiscal year ends in September. Products include iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Wearables, Home and Accessories, including AirPods, Apple TV, Apple Watch, Beats, HomePod mini, and accessories.

title: Services, Markets, and Distribution
key_items: Advertising; AppleCare; Cloud Services; Digital Content; Payment Services
summary: Apple’s services include advertising through its own platforms and third-party licensing; fee-based AppleCare technical support, repairs, replacements, and, in some cases, damage or loss coverage; cloud storage and syncing; platforms for apps and digital content; subscription offerings for games, fitness, music, news, and original video and live sports; and Apple Card and Apple Pay. Customers span consumer, business, education, enterprise, and government markets. Apple sells its and third-party products through retail and online stores, direct sales, and indirect channels; in 2022, these generated 38% and 62% of net sales, respectively.

title: Competition
summary: The text describes intense competition driven by pricing, rapid innovation, short product cycles, and rivals’ broad resources, low-cost strategies, imitation, and intellectual-property infringement; Apple’s success depends on timely innovation and factors including price, quality, features, ecosystem, distribution, support, and reputation. It notes component shortages, limited suppliers, custom-component and capacity risks, supply-agreement uncertainty, and outsourced manufacturing, primarily in Asia. Apple invests in R&D, licensing, and acquisitions. It holds and actively protects a broad global IP portfolio, but relies chiefly on its personnel and also depends on third-party IP licenses whose future availability and terms are uncertain.

title: Competition, Components, R&D, and Intellectual Property
summary: The Company faces intense competition across its product and service markets, including price pressure, imitation, integrated rival offerings, and free or illegitimate content models. Components may be limited to few suppliers, subject to shortages and price fluctuations, or constrained by custom manufacturing capacity; supply agreements may not continue, and most hardware is made by outsourcing partners, mainly in Asia. Competitiveness depends on timely innovation through R&D, licensing, and acquisitions. The Company protects a broad global IP portfolio but relies chiefly on its people, and may need third-party licenses that could become unavailable or costly.

title: Business Seasonality, Human Capital, and Investor Information
key_items: Business Seasonality and Product Introductions; Available Information
Workplace Practices and Policies; Compensation and Benefits; Inclusion and Diversity; Engagement; Health and Safety
summary: Apple describes seasonal sales patterns and how product launches affect sales, costs, and channel inventory. It reports about 164,000 full-time equivalent employees and outlines its commitments to equal opportunity, inclusive and safe workplaces, competitive compensation, employee benefits and development, diversity, engagement, and health and safety, including pandemic measures. The page also explains where SEC filings and investor information are available and clarifies that website content is not incorporated into the filing.

title: Item 1A. Risk Factors
summary: The Company’s business, reputation, operating results, financial condition, and stock price may be materially harmed by known or unknown risks. Past performance is not a reliable guide to future results, and historical trends should not be used to predict them; the risk-factor discussion includes forward-looking statements and should be read alongside the relevant MD&A and consolidated financial statements and notes in the Form 10-K.

title: Macroeconomic and Industry Risks
key_items: The Company’s operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions and adverse economic conditions can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.
The Company’s business, results of operations, financial condition and stock price have been adversely affected and could in the future be materially adversely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Company’s business can be impacted by political events, trade and other international disputes, war, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues, industrial accidents and other business interruptions.
Global markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and subject to rapid technological change, and the Company may be unable to compete effectively in these markets.
summary: The text outlines Apple’s risks from adverse global and regional economic conditions, which can weaken demand, disrupt suppliers and partners, impair receivables, financing, liquidity and investments, and harm results and stock price. COVID-19 has caused economic, supply-chain and demand disruptions; future effects remain uncertain, may impede operations and strategy, and can amplify other risks. Political conflict, trade restrictions, tariffs, disasters, climate-related events, accidents, cyberattacks, labor issues and public-health emergencies can disrupt manufacturing, supply, sales and services; recovery may be costly, and insurance may be inadequate. Finally, intense competition, rapid technological change, price pressure, limited market share, imitation and uneven intellectual-property protection threaten Apple’s ability to innovate, earn returns and maintain product, service and design advantages.

title: Business Risks

nodes.title: Product Transition and Outsourcing Risks
key_items: To remain competitive and stimulate customer demand, the Company must successfully manage frequent introductions and transitions of products and services.
The Company depends on component and product manufacturing and logistical services provided by outsourcing partners, many of which are located outside of the U.S.
nodes.summary: The Company’s competitiveness depends on successfully developing, introducing, and transitioning products and services amid risks involving market acceptance, production ramp-ups, software, inventory, supply, cost, and quality. It relies on concentrated outsourcing partners—many outside the U.S.—for manufacturing, components, assembly, and logistics, limiting direct control and creating risks to supply, quality, flexibility, and reputation, including supplier-code violations and product-defect liabilities. Disasters, system failures, disputes, and other disruptions may affect operations; partner financial distress may reduce supply and jeopardize recovery of equipment investments and supplier prepayments.

nodes.title: Future operating results depend upon the Company’s ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks to Apple from component shortages, single-source suppliers, price volatility, semiconductor constraints, supplier financial distress, and difficulty renewing supply agreements, potentially delaying production and harming results. Product and service design or manufacturing defects, outages, and quality failures may cause safety hazards, liability, recalls, costs, lost sales, and reputational damage. Rapid obsolescence and inaccurate forecasts may require inventory or asset write-downs, cancellation fees, or leave purchase commitments unused. Apple also depends on third-party intellectual-property licenses, which may be unavailable or costly and could restrict sales or materially affect its business.

nodes.title: Product, Supply, Asset, and Intellectual Property Risks
key_items: The Company’s products and services may be affected from time to time by design and manufacturing defects that could materially adversely affect the Company’s business and result in harm to the Company’s reputation.
The Company is exposed to the risk of write-downs on the value of its inventory and other assets, in addition to purchase commitment cancellation risk.
The Company relies on access to third-party intellectual property, which may not be available to the Company on commercially reasonable terms or at all.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from reliance on single-source components, supplier capacity constraints, and shipment delays; product and service defects, outages, safety issues, liability, recalls, costs, lost sales, and reputational harm; inventory obsolescence, asset impairments, cancellation fees, and inaccurate forecasts or unused purchase commitments; and dependence on third-party intellectual property, including infringement claims and the possibility that licenses are unavailable or costly, limiting sales and harming financial results.

nodes.title: Third-Party Software and Digital Content Risks
key_items: The Company’s future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers.

Failure to obtain or create digital content that appeals to the Company’s customers, or to make such content available on commercially reasonable terms, could have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.
nodes.summary: Apple’s performance depends on developers continuing to create and maintain appealing applications for its products; its minority market share and rapid technological change may limit app availability, quality, and customer satisfaction. App Store business, commissions, and distribution could be affected by business changes, EU legislation, litigation, and investigations. Apple also risks losing access to third-party content or facing higher costs and restrictive terms, while producing original content is costly and may not appeal to customers. Production constraints, including those caused by COVID-19, and evolving digital-rights security requirements may add costs or prove difficult to meet.

nodes.title: Workforce, Reseller, and Technology Risks
key_items: The Company’s success depends largely on the talents and efforts of its team members, the continued service and availability of highly skilled employees, including key personnel, and the Company’s ability to nurture its distinctive and inclusive culture.
The Company depends on the performance of carriers, wholesalers, retailers and other resellers.
The Company’s business and reputation are impacted by information technology system failures and network disruptions.
nodes.summary: The Company’s success relies on retaining skilled employees and key leaders, managing changing workforce dynamics, and preserving its distinctive, inclusive culture; failures could harm recruitment, operations, reputation, and financial performance. Product sales depend on carriers, wholesalers, retailers, and resellers, whose financing offers, financial health, distribution, and marketing may change; investments in reseller programs do not guarantee returns. IT or network disruptions affecting the Company or its supply chain—from disasters, outages, or cyber incidents—may defeat continuity measures, interrupt services, transactions, manufacturing, or shipping, and materially harm the business, reputation, results, and financial condition.

nodes.title: Losses or unauthorized access to or releases of confidential information, including personal information, could subject the Company to significant reputational, financial, legal and operational consequences.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from loss, disclosure, or unauthorized access to confidential and personal information, including attacks on the Company and its suppliers, imperfect security controls, phishing, customer-access disruptions, legal and reputational harm, and potentially inadequate insurance. It also warns that high visibility and valuable data make the Company a target. New strategies and acquisitions may distract management, incur unexpected costs or liabilities, face regulatory hurdles, fail, or impair assets. Retail stores require substantial investment and leases; weak sales, closures, pandemic measures, operating costs, economic conditions, partner relationships, inventory fluctuations, and lease availability could adversely affect results.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity, Strategic Investments, and Retail Risks
key_items: Investment in new business strategies and acquisitions could disrupt the Company’s ongoing business, present risks not originally contemplated and materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition.
The Company’s retail stores have required and will continue to require a substantial investment and commitment of resources and are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from frequent, increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, heightened targeting, potentially inadequate safeguards and insurance, and customer access disruptions. It also warns that new strategies and acquisitions can distract management, incur unexpected costs or regulatory barriers, fail to deliver returns, and harm results. Retail stores require substantial investment and lease commitments; weak sales, closures, high operating costs, economic conditions, and challenges managing construction, partners, inventory, or leases could adversely affect performance and finances.

summary: The section covers risks to competitiveness and results from product transitions, outsourced manufacturing, supplier concentration, component shortages, cost volatility, defects, outages, recalls, obsolescence, forecasting, and third-party intellectual-property licenses. It also addresses dependence on app developers and digital content; workforce retention and culture; reseller and carrier relationships; operational, supply-chain, and cybersecurity disruptions and data breaches; strategic investments and acquisitions; and retail investment, leases, costs, and sales.

title: Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks
key_items: The Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition could be adversely impacted by unfavorable results of legal proceedings or government investigations.
The Company is subject to complex and changing laws and regulations worldwide, which exposes the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.

Expectations relating to environmental, social and governance considerations expose the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs, reputational harm, and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.

The technology industry, including, in some instances, the Company, is subject to intense media, political and regulatory scrutiny, which exposes the Company to increasing regulation, government investigations, legal actions and penalties.
The Company’s business is subject to a variety of U.S. and international laws, rules, policies and other obligations regarding data protection.
summary: The Company faces growing litigation, investigations, indemnity claims and patent disputes; outcomes may bring substantial damages, injunctions, settlements, operating restrictions, costs or reputational and financial harm, with insurance potentially insufficient. Complex, changing global laws may raise costs, constrain products and operations, or cause penalties and import delays. ESG commitments create implementation, compliance and stakeholder-expectation risks. Technology-sector scrutiny, antitrust and App Store investigations, legislation, litigation, and partners’ legal troubles may force business changes and harm demand, privacy perceptions and competitiveness. Worldwide privacy and data-protection rules—including heightened duties for health, financial, biometric and payment-card data—require costly compliance; violations may trigger audits, fines, liability, higher processing costs or loss of card-processing capability.

title: Financial Risks
key_items: The Company expects its quarterly net sales and results of operations to fluctuate.
The Company’s financial performance is subject to risks associated with changes in the value of the U.S. dollar relative to local currencies.
The Company is exposed to credit risk and fluctuations in the values of its investment portfolio.

The Company is exposed to credit risk on its trade accounts receivable, vendor non-trade receivables and prepayments related to long-term supply agreements, and this risk is heightened during periods when economic conditions worsen.
The Company is subject to changes in tax rates, the adoption of new U.S. or international tax legislation and exposure to additional tax liabilities.
summary: The filing describes financial risks including quarterly and seasonal sales fluctuations, product concentration, margin pressures, unexpected operational disruptions, currency exposure and imperfect hedging, investment-value and customer/vendor credit risks, and changing tax laws, rates, audits and liabilities. General risks include stock-price volatility and expectations for growth, dividends and repurchases. It reports no unresolved staff comments; identifies Cupertino headquarters and facilities considered suitable; summarizes the Epic App Store antitrust litigation and other ordinary-course legal matters; and states mine-safety disclosures are not applicable.

title: Risk Factors, Properties, and Legal Proceedings
key_items: The price of the Company’s stock is subject to volatility.
Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments; Item 2. Properties
summary: The text discusses tax examination risks and potential adverse effects of higher tax liabilities, stock-price volatility and expectations for growth, dividends, and repurchases, and states there are no unresolved staff comments. It describes the Company’s Cupertino headquarters and U.S. and international facilities. It summarizes the Epic Games App Store antitrust case, rulings, injunction, and appeals, plus other ordinary-course legal matters, settlements, and potential financial impacts of unfavorable outcomes.

title: Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures
summary: Item 4 reports that mine safety disclosures are not applicable. Item 5 states Apple’s stock trades on Nasdaq as AAPL and that it had 23,838 shareholders of record on October 14, 2022. For the quarter ended September 24, 2022, Apple repurchased 160.172 million shares through open-market and privately negotiated purchases at the listed monthly average prices. Its board-authorized buyback program permits up to $405 billion in repurchases; $344.3 billion had been used, with no minimum purchase obligation and transactions permitted under Rule 10b5-1 plans.

title: Stock Market, Shareholders, and Repurchases
key_items: Item 5. Market for Registrant’s Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities
Purchases of Equity Securities by the Issuer and Affiliated Purchasers
summary: Apple common stock trades on Nasdaq under AAPL, and the company had 23,838 shareholders of record as of October 14, 2022. The page reports share repurchases by period for the three months ended September 24, 2022, including shares purchased and average prices. As of September 24, Apple was authorized to repurchase up to $405 billion; $344.3 billion had been used. The program has no minimum purchase requirement and permits open-market or privately negotiated transactions, including Rule 10b5-1 plans.

title: Stock Performance and Reserved Item 6
summary: Compares five-year cumulative total shareholder returns through September 24, 2022, for Apple and three indexes, assuming $100 invested on September 29, 2017 with dividends reinvested. The page includes annual performance data, notes that past performance does not predict future results, and provides index data-source copyrights. Item 6 is reserved.

title: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
summary: Item 7’s MD&A should be read with the consolidated financial statements and notes in Part II, Item 8. It generally covers fiscal 2022 and 2021 and their year-to-year comparisons; discussion of 2020 and comparisons between 2021 and 2020 are omitted and available in the company’s 2021 Form 10-K, Part II, Item 7.

title: Fiscal Year Highlights
key_items: iPhone; Mac; iPad; Wearables, Home and Accessories; Services
summary: Apple’s fiscal 2022 net sales rose 8% ($28.5 billion), mainly from iPhone, Services and Mac, while a strong U.S. dollar negatively affected sales across categories. The text lists quarterly product, service and software announcements, including new Macs, iPhones, iPads, AirPods, Apple Watch models, operating systems and Apple Pay Later. Apple increased its share-repurchase authorization to $405 billion and its quarterly dividend to $0.23; it repurchased $90.2 billion of stock and paid $14.8 billion in dividends. It describes COVID-19’s economic, operational and potential business impacts, including supplier and logistics disruptions. Sales tables and notes define product and service categories; year over year, iPhone, Mac, Wearables/Home/Accessories and Services sales increased, while iPad sales declined, with reasons given for each category.

title: Segment Operating Performance
key_items: Products Gross Margin; Services Gross Margin
summary: The Company reports five geographic segments—Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific—with defined regional coverage and separate management reflecting customer, distribution and market differences; further details are in Note 11. The text presents 2020–2022 segment sales and explains 2022 changes: sales rose in all regions except Japan, driven mainly by iPhone, Services and, in some regions, Mac; currency movements affected regional results. It reports product and services gross margins and percentages, which generally increased in 2022 due to mix, volume, sales and leverage, partly offset by currency weakness; future margins may be volatile and face downward pressure. Operating expenses and percentages are shown for 2020–2022; 2022 R&D growth reflected headcount and engineering costs, while SG&A growth reflected headcount, advertising and professional services.

title: Operating Expenses
summary: The text reports Apple’s 2022, 2021 and 2020 gross margins and percentages: product margins rose in 2022 due to mix and volume, and services margins due to sales, leverage and mix; both were partly offset by currency weakness. It warns that future margins face volatility and downward pressure. Operating expenses increased, driven by headcount, engineering programs, advertising and professional services. Other income/expense declined due to securities losses, equity valuation adjustments and interest expense, partly offset by foreign-exchange gains. It provides income-tax provisions and rates, explaining effective-rate differences across years through foreign earnings, tax benefits, credits, deductions and state taxes. Apple says cash and securities, operating cash flow and debt-market access will meet needs and capital returns. Cash obligations include notes and interest, commercial paper, and lease payments, with amounts and portions due within 12 months specified.

title: Provision for Income Taxes
summary: The text reports 2022–2020 other income/expense and income-tax results. Net other expense was $334 million in 2022, versus income of $258 million in 2021 and $803 million in 2020; the 2022 decline versus 2021 reflected higher realized debt-security losses, unfavorable equity-security fair-value adjustments, and higher interest expense, partly offset by foreign-exchange gains. Income-tax provisions were $19.3 billion in 2022, $9.68 billion in 2021, and $14.527 billion in 2020; effective tax rates were 16.2%, 13.3%, and 14.4%, respectively, against a 21% federal statutory rate. Rates were below statutory levels mainly due to foreign earnings, share-based compensation, and applicable R&D or foreign-derived intangible income benefits, partly offset by state taxes. The 2022 rate rose versus 2021 because of higher tax on foreign earnings, Treasury guidance affecting foreign tax credits, and lower foreign-derived income and share-based compensation benefits.

title: Liquidity and Capital Resources
key_items: Manufacturing Purchase Obligations; Other Purchase Obligations; Deemed Repatriation Tax Payable
summary: The Company expects $156.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and unrestricted marketable securities, operating cash flow and debt-market access to cover cash needs and capital returns for the next 12 months and beyond. At September 24, 2022, obligations included $111.8 billion in fixed-rate debt ($11.1 billion due within a year) and $41.3 billion in interest ($2.9 billion due within a year); $10.0 billion in commercial paper due within a year; $15.3 billion in lease payments ($2.0 billion due within a year); $71.1 billion in primarily noncancelable manufacturing commitments ($68.4 billion due within a year); $17.8 billion in other purchase obligations ($6.8 billion due within a year); and $22.0 billion in deemed repatriation tax ($5.3 billion due within a year). Manufacturing arrangements rely on outsourcing partners and supplier components, with demand information typically covering up to 150 days. The Board-authorized capital return program has no minimum share-purchase requirement; the quarterly dividend was $0.23 per share, with annual increases intended subject to Board declaration.

title: Critical Accounting Estimates
summary: Management’s GAAP financial reporting relies on estimates and judgments based on experience and reasonable assumptions. Significant estimates concern uncertain tax positions across U.S. and foreign jurisdictions and ordinary-course legal claims; reserve outcomes may materially differ from expectations. The text also describes market-risk management: derivatives may not fully offset exposures or align in timing. Interest-rate risk affects investments and debt; a 100-basis-point rise could reduce portfolio fair value by $4.0 billion (2022) or $4.1 billion (2021), with losses realized upon early sale, and increase annual debt interest expense by $201 million or $186 million, respectively. Foreign-currency strength can reduce dollar-reported sales and margins and pressure local pricing. The Company uses forwards and options to hedge selected exposures, generally forecast revenue and inventory for up to 12 months, but may leave some risks unhedged.

title: Market Risk and Interest Rate Management
key_items: Interest Rate and Foreign Currency Risk Management
summary: The Company reviews foreign-exchange forwards and options and interest-rate swaps, which may only partly offset exposure and may produce gains or losses at different times from underlying exposures, affecting results. Interest-rate exposure mainly involves investments and debt, especially U.S. rates. Its conservative, investment-grade portfolio strategy limits issuer exposure; a 100-basis-point rate increase would reduce portfolio fair value by $4.0 billion in 2022 and $4.1 billion in 2021, with losses realized only if securities are sold before maturity. Debt carrying amounts were $110.1 billion in 2022 and $118.7 billion in 2021. Swaps manage debt-rate risk, generally offsetting debt gains and losses; a 100-basis-point increase would raise annualized interest expense by $201 million and $186 million, respectively.

title: Foreign Currency Risk
summary: The Company’s net foreign-currency receipts mean a stronger U.S. dollar can reduce reported sales and gross margins, while volatility may force local-price adjustments. It may use forwards and options to hedge existing balances, commitments, forecast cash flows, subsidiary investments, and debt-related currency effects; revenue and inventory exposures are typically hedged for up to 12 months, though some risks remain unhedged for accounting or cost reasons. A Monte Carlo VAR analysis, excluding underlying exposures, estimated a 95%-confidence maximum one-day derivative fair-value loss of $1.0 billion in 2022 versus $550 million in 2021; hedging gains and losses generally offset underlying changes. Actual results may differ materially because of forecasting limitations.

title: Item 8. Financial Statements and Supplementary Data
summary: Item 8 indexes Apple’s consolidated financial statements: statements of operations, comprehensive income, shareholders’ equity, and cash flows for fiscal years 2020–2022; balance sheets for 2021 and 2022; notes; and independent auditors’ reports, with page references. Financial statement schedules are omitted because they are inapplicable, immaterial, or covered in the statements and notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated statements of operations present results for fiscal years ended September 25, 2021, September 24, 2022, and September 26, 2020, in millions except share counts (thousands) and per-share amounts. They report product and services sales, cost of sales, gross margin, research and development and selling, general and administrative expenses, operating income, other income or expense, pretax income, income-tax provision, net income, basic and diluted earnings per share, and corresponding weighted shares. The statements refer readers to the accompanying financial-statement notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income report net income, other comprehensive income or loss, and total comprehensive income for fiscal years ended September 24, 2022, September 25, 2021, and September 26, 2020. Other comprehensive items include foreign currency translation, derivative fair-value changes and realized gains or losses, and marketable debt-security fair-value changes and realized gains or losses, all net of tax. The statements refer readers to the accompanying financial-statement notes.

title: Apple Inc. Consolidated Balance Sheets
summary: Apple’s consolidated balance sheets as of September 24, 2022 and September 25, 2021 report current and non-current assets, including cash, securities, receivables, inventory, property and other assets; current and non-current liabilities, including payables, debt and deferred revenue; commitments and contingencies; and shareholders’ equity, detailing share authorization, issued and outstanding shares, paid-in capital, retained earnings and accumulated comprehensive income or loss. Amounts are in millions except share counts (thousands) and par value.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF SHAREHOLDERS’ EQUITY
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of shareholders’ equity report beginning and ending total equity for fiscal years 2020–2022, with changes in common stock and additional paid-in capital, retained earnings or accumulated deficit, and accumulated other comprehensive income or loss. Changes include stock issuance, share-based compensation, net income, dividends, equity-award share withholding, repurchases, and accounting-principle changes. Dividends declared per share or RSU are also listed; amounts are in millions except per-share figures, with notes referenced.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS (intro)
nodes.summary: Apple’s consolidated cash flow statements report operating, investing, and financing activities for fiscal years 2020–2022, including net income adjustments, changes in operating assets and liabilities, investment purchases and proceeds, capital expenditures and acquisitions, dividends, share repurchases, debt and commercial paper activity, and resulting cash decreases and balances. Supplemental disclosures show cash paid for income taxes and interest; the statements refer to accompanying notes and Note 1 on significant accounting policies.

nodes.title: Basis of Presentation and Preparation
nodes.summary: Apple’s consolidated financial statements cover the Company and its wholly owned subsidiaries, eliminate intercompany accounts and transactions, and are prepared under U.S. GAAP using estimates that may differ from actual results; prior-period figures were reclassified where needed for consistent presentation. Apple’s fiscal year ends on the last Saturday of September and spans 52 or 53 weeks, with an extra week added in the first quarter every five or six years to align with calendar quarters. Fiscal 2022, 2021, and 2020 each had 52 weeks; references to years and periods mean Apple fiscal periods unless otherwise stated.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition
nodes.summary: The text outlines Apple’s accounting policies for revenue recognition, including transfer timing, sales reductions, allocating prices among performance obligations, bundled services and upgrades, undelivered long-term services, gross versus net third-party sales, and sales taxes. It also describes share-based compensation measurement and expense recognition; 2022–2020 basic and diluted EPS computations and the treasury-stock method; classification and accounting of cash equivalents and marketable securities, including cost basis; and FIFO inventory measurement.

nodes.title: Revenue, Compensation, EPS, Investments and Inventory Policies
nodes.summary: The text explains gross versus net revenue recognition for third-party products and treatment of customer taxes; share-based compensation measurement and expense recognition; basic and diluted EPS calculations for 2022–2020 using the treasury stock method; classification and accounting policies for cash equivalents and marketable securities, including cost determination; and FIFO inventory measurement.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies and Measurements
nodes.summary: The page explains how restricted securities are classified; depreciation and software amortization methods, useful lives, and expenses; derivative fair-value recognition, hedge accounting, excluded components, presentation, and cash-flow classification; valuation methods for financial instruments; deferred taxes tied to the U.S. minimum tax on certain foreign earnings; and the treatment of lease and nonlease components and lease discount rates.

nodes.title: Segment Reporting
nodes.summary: The Company uses management’s internal decision-making and performance reports to identify segments, organized geographically into Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific, with specified regional boundaries. Though offering similar products and services, segments are managed separately to reflect customer and distribution locations and local market conditions; they use the same accounting policies. Performance is measured by net sales and operating income. Sales generally follow customer or retail-store location; segment income includes third-party sales, directly attributable costs and expenses, and generally advertising incurred in the region. It excludes other income and expense, centrally managed costs (including R&D, corporate marketing, certain share-based compensation, taxes, nonrecurring charges, and other general and administrative costs), and intersegment transfers.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Revenue
nodes.summary: Note 2 reports net sales by product and service for 2020–2022, explains included deferred software and service revenue, identifies Wearables/Home/Accessories and Services categories, and notes prior-year deferred revenue recognized. Revenue mix was generally consistent by segment, except for a higher iPhone share in Greater China in 2021–2022. Deferred revenue was $12.4 billion in 2022 versus $11.9 billion in 2021, with expected realization timing disclosed. Note 3 details 2022 and 2021 cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities by investment category, fair-value hierarchy, adjusted cost, gains/losses and balance-sheet classification; identifies restricted securities and explains Level 1 and Level 2 valuation inputs. It also presents 2022 non-current debt securities’ fair values by contractual maturity.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments and Hedging
nodes.summary: The Company uses derivatives to partially manage foreign-exchange and interest-rate risks, though it may leave exposures unhedged and hedges cannot be assured to fully offset losses. It describes foreign-exchange hedges for forecast revenue, inventory purchases, foreign-currency debt and securities, including designated cash-flow or fair-value hedges and undesignated instruments; forecast exposures are typically hedged up to 12 months, while term-debt cash-flow exposure may be hedged up to 20 years. Interest-rate swaps, options and other instruments may hedge debt or securities. The text reports 2022 and 2021 derivative notionals, 2022 gross derivative asset and liability fair values and their Level 2 balance-sheet classification. It explains collateral and master netting arrangements, which could reduce both assets and liabilities by $7.8 billion, leaving a net derivative asset of $412 million, and introduces carrying amounts of items in fair-value hedges.

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable
nodes.summary: Trade receivables are owed by carriers and diverse business and consumer customers; the company generally requires no collateral but may use collateral, credit support, insurance, or third-party financing, with no usual recourse or shared credit risk. In 2022, one customer represented 10% of trade receivables; carriers represented 44%, versus 42% in 2021. Vendor non-trade receivables arise from component sales to manufacturing vendors; major vendors accounted for 54% and 13% in 2022, and 52%, 11%, and 11% in 2021. The text also introduces financial statement details and a property, plant, and equipment table covering asset categories, gross value, accumulated depreciation, and net value.

nodes.title: Other Non-Current Liabilities
nodes.summary:
Other Non-Current Liabilities
Long-term taxes payable Other non-current liabilities Total other non-current liabilities

nodes.title: Other Income/(Expense), Net
nodes.summary: Presents Apple’s other income and expense components for 2020–2022, followed by Note 5 on income taxes. It details federal, state, and foreign current and deferred tax provisions and totals for each year, reports foreign pretax earnings, and introduces a reconciliation of tax provision to the 21% federal statutory rate, including state taxes, the Act, foreign subsidiary earnings, deductions, credits, equity-award tax benefits, other items, and effective tax rates.

nodes.title: Deferred Tax Assets and Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text presents Apple’s 2020–2022 deferred-tax reconciliation figures and its deferred tax assets and liabilities at September 24, 2022 and September 25, 2021. It lists asset categories, valuation allowances, liability categories, and net deferred tax assets. For 2022, net deferred tax assets were $14.537 billion. Apple also reports $4.4 billion in Irish foreign tax credit carryforwards and $2.5 billion in California R&D credit carryforwards, both available indefinitely, with valuation allowances against these credits and some other temporary differences.

nodes.title: Tax Uncertainties and European State Aid
nodes.summary: The Company reported gross unrecognized tax benefits of $16.8 billion in 2022 ($8.0 billion affecting its effective tax rate if recognized), compared with $15.5 billion in 2021 ($6.6 billion rate impact). A table details 2020–2022 balance changes. Tax returns remain subject to examination in certain jurisdictions, and benefits could decrease by up to $4.8 billion within 12 months. The European Commission’s 2016 decision concerning Irish tax opinions sought recovery of €13.1 billion plus interest for 2003–2014; the General Court annulled it in 2020, and the Commission appealed. The Company believes any related Irish taxes may qualify for U.S. tax credits. The adjusted recovery amount was €12.7 billion excluding interest, funded in restricted escrow pending legal proceedings.

nodes.title: Note 6 – Leases
nodes.summary: The note describes leases for equipment and corporate, data-center, manufacturing, and retail facilities, generally lasting up to 10 years with renewal options. It reports fixed and output-based variable lease costs and fixed cash payments for 2020–2022, plus noncash ROU assets obtained for lease liabilities, including Topic 842 adoption effects. It presents 2021–2022 operating and finance ROU assets and liabilities by financial-statement line, 2022 lease-liability maturities and imputed interest, remaining lease terms and discount rates, and $1.2 billion of uncommenced future lease payments beginning in 2023–2026.

nodes.title: Commercial Paper and Repurchase Agreements
nodes.summary: The Company issues unsecured commercial paper for general corporate purposes, including dividends and share repurchases. Outstanding balances were $10.0 billion in 2022 and $6.0 billion in 2021, generally maturing within nine months, with weighted-average rates of 2.31% and 0.06%, respectively. The text reports commercial-paper proceeds and repayments for 2020–2022, including net cash flows. In 2020, the Company also entered into $5.2 billion of repurchase agreements involving marketable securities, accounted for as collateralized borrowings due to its continuing involvement; all were settled by September 26, 2020.

nodes.title: Term Debt
nodes.summary: The text summarizes Apple’s term debt in 2022 and 2021, including note types, maturities, rates, carrying-value adjustments, current and noncurrent portions, hedging to manage interest-rate and currency risk, interest expense, future principal payments, and fair values. It reports 2022 share repurchases and common-stock balance changes for 2020–2022. It also describes the 2022 Employee Stock Plan’s award types, vesting, share-count rules, dividend rights, and authorization, and notes that new grants under the 2014 plan ended in 2022.

nodes.title: Debt, Shareholders’ Equity, and Employee Stock Plans
nodes.summary: The page reports future principal payments and fair values of the Company’s Notes. It describes 2022 share repurchases, the program’s nonbinding nature and permitted transaction methods, and common-stock share changes for 2020–2022. It also summarizes the 2022 Employee Stock Plan’s eligible awards, RSU vesting, share-count rules, dividend equivalent rights, and authorized shares, and notes that the 2014 Plan offered similar awards plus cash bonuses before new grants were ended in 2022.

nodes.title: Apple Director, Employee Stock, and 401(k) Plans
key_items: Apple Inc. Non-Employee Director Stock Plan
nodes.summary: Apple’s shareholder-approved Director Plan permits stock options and RSUs for non-employee directors, with automatic initial and annual RSU grants and Board authority to adjust award values, mix, and share calculations within plan limits. RSUs count twice against available shares, carry dividend equivalent rights, and the plan expires November 12, 2027; about 45 million shares were authorized. The Purchase Plan lets substantially all employees buy stock through payroll deductions at 85% of the lower offering-period start or end value, subject to 10% compensation and $25,000 annual limits; about 230 million shares were authorized. Under the tax-qualified 401(k) Plan, U.S. employees may contribute within legal and plan limits, and Apple matches 50%–100% based on service, up to 6% of eligible earnings.

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Units
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s 2020–2022 RSU grants, vesting, cancellations, balances, and grant-date fair values; vest-date fair values, tax-withheld shares, and related tax remittances; annual share-based compensation expense and tax benefits; and $16.7 billion in unrecognized RSU and stock-option compensation expected to be recognized over 2.6 years. It also describes supply-source, component-shortage, pricing, custom-component, manufacturing, and supplier-capacity risks; $27.286 billion in future unconditional purchase obligations; and management’s view that unresolved legal claims were not reasonably likely to cause a material loss beyond recorded accruals.

nodes.title: Compensation and Commitments
key_items: Concentrations in the Available Sources of Supply of Materials and Product
nodes.summary: Reports share-based compensation expense and related tax benefits for 2020–2022, plus $16.7 billion in unrecognized RSU and stock-option costs expected to be recognized over 2.6 years. Describes supply risks from single-source and custom components, shortages, price fluctuations, capacity constraints, and outsourced manufacturing mainly in Asia. Lists unconditional purchase obligations for suppliers, internet services, and content, totaling $27.286 billion.

nodes.title: Contingencies
nodes.summary: The Company reports unresolved ordinary-course legal claims, but management believes no material loss is reasonably possible beyond recorded accruals. Segment information presents 2020–2022 net sales and operating income for the Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific, plus reconciliations of segment operating income to consolidated operating income. Geographic data shows U.S. and China (including Hong Kong and Taiwan) were the only countries exceeding 10% of sales in those years, and reports net sales and long-lived assets by U.S., China, and other countries; China’s long-lived assets mainly support manufacturing, retail, and related infrastructure.

nodes.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
key_items: Opinion on the Financial Statements; Basis for Opinion; Critical Audit Matter
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young’s report gives an unqualified opinion that Apple’s 2020–2022 financial statements fairly present its financial position, results, and cash flows under U.S. GAAP, and notes a separate unqualified opinion on internal controls. It explains management’s and auditor’s responsibilities and the PCAOB audit basis. The critical audit matter is uncertain tax positions: $16.8 billion in gross unrecognized benefits, including $8.0 billion affecting the tax rate. Auditors tested related controls and evaluated management analyses, tax-authority communications, legal and tax advice, and disclosures. EY has served as auditor since 2009; report dated October 27, 2022.

summary: Presents Apple’s 2020–2022 consolidated cash flows and financial-statement notes, covering accounting basis and policies; revenue, segments, investments, derivatives, receivables, taxes, leases, debt, equity, employee plans, compensation, commitments, and contingencies; and related financial tables and disclosures. It also includes the independent auditor’s unqualified opinions, audit responsibilities, and critical audit matter concerning uncertain tax positions.

title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm

nodes.title: Apple Internal Control Audit Report
key_items: Opinion on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young reports that Apple maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of September 24, 2022, under COSO criteria, and notes its separate unqualified opinion on Apple’s financial statements. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, independence, PCAOB audit standards, procedures, and reasonable-assurance basis. It defines the controls’ purpose and key safeguards, while noting that controls may not prevent or detect misstatements and that effectiveness may change over time. Signed in San Jose on October 27, 2022.

nodes.title: Accounting Changes and Internal Controls
key_items: Item 9. Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants on Accounting and Financial Disclosure
Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures
Management’s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The company reported no changes or disagreements with accountants. Management found disclosure controls effective as of September 24, 2022. The page describes internal controls’ purposes and inherent limits: they provide reasonable, not absolute, assurance, may not prevent or detect all errors or fraud, and can weaken as conditions or compliance change. Management assessed financial reporting controls using the 2013 COSO framework and concluded they were effective on that date; Ernst & Young issued an audit report included in Part II, Item 8.

nodes.title: Changes in Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Apple reported no fourth-quarter 2022 changes in internal controls over financial reporting that materially affected or were likely to materially affect those controls. Five officers had Rule 10b5-1 equity trading plans during the quarter, which set terms for future stock transactions. Foreign-jurisdiction inspection disclosure was not applicable. Information on directors and governance, executive compensation, security ownership and stockholder matters, related transactions and director independence, and auditor fees and services would be provided in the 2023 proxy statement and incorporated by reference.

nodes.title: Trading Plans and Part III Disclosures
key_items: Rule 10b5-1 Trading Plans; Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Item 10. Directors, Executive Officers and Corporate Governance
Item 12. Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management and Related Stockholder Matters
Item 13. Certain Relationships and Related Transactions, and Director Independence
Item 14. Principal Accountant Fees and Services
nodes.summary: Reports that five Apple officers had Rule 10b5-1 trading plans during the three months ended September 24, 2022, and briefly explains these plans. Item 9C on foreign jurisdictions preventing inspections is not applicable. Part III items on directors and governance, executive compensation, security ownership, related-party transactions and director independence, and auditor fees and services are incorporated by reference to the 2023 Proxy Statement.

nodes.title: PART IV
key_items: (3) Exhibits required by Item 601 of Regulation S-K (1)
nodes.summary: Part IV, Item 15 lists the report’s consolidated financial statements, notes, and independent auditor’s reports for fiscal years 2020–2022, with page references; financial statement schedules are omitted as inapplicable, immaterial, or included elsewhere. It inventories exhibits, including corporate charter and bylaws, securities descriptions, debt indentures and note certificates from 2013–2022, compensation and equity plans and award agreements, subsidiaries, auditor consent, power of attorney, executive certifications, and Inline XBRL files, with incorporation-by-reference details and filing notes. Item 16 states there is no Form 10-K summary.

summary: Ernst & Young’s unqualified audit reports that Apple’s internal control over financial reporting was effective as of September 24, 2022, under COSO criteria, and describes management and auditor responsibilities, audit procedures, control purposes, and inherent limits. Apple reported effective disclosure controls, no accountant disagreements or material fourth-quarter control changes, and five officers with Rule 10b5-1 trading plans. The section notes that foreign-jurisdiction inspection disclosure is inapplicable, incorporates specified Part III disclosures from the 2023 proxy statement, and lists Part IV financial statements, omitted schedules, exhibits, and the absence of a Form 10-K summary.

title: SIGNATURES
summary: Apple’s October 27, 2022 Form 10-K is signed under the Securities Exchange Act by CFO Luca Maestri on the company’s behalf. The text grants Timothy D. Cook and Luca Maestri joint and several power of attorney to sign and file amendments and related documents. It lists the report’s signatories, their roles—including executive, financial, and accounting officers and directors—and their signature date of October 27, 2022.

title: DESCRIPTION OF THE REGISTRANT’S SECURITIES REGISTERED PURSUANT TO SECTION 12 OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934
summary: As of September 24, 2022, Apple had 11 securities registered under Exchange Act Section 12: common stock and 10 note issues with maturities from 2022 to 2042 and coupon rates ranging from 0% to 3.6%. All were listed on The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC.

title: DESCRIPTION OF COMMON STOCK
key_items: Dividends; Right to Receive Liquidation Distributions; No Preemptive or Similar Rights
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law; Listing
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law
summary: The text summarizes Apple’s common-stock rights under its Articles, Bylaws, and California law: 50.4 billion shares are authorized, and outstanding shares are fully paid and nonassessable. Each share has one noncumulative vote; it describes approval thresholds, director elections, removal and vacancy-filling, amendments, and meeting adjournments. Shareholders may receive board-declared dividends and pro rata liquidation distributions, but have no preemptive, conversion, redemption, or sinking-fund rights. It outlines anti-takeover provisions on director vacancies, shareholder notices and nominations, proxy access, and special meetings, plus California’s interested-party transaction fairness-opinion requirement. The stock trades on Nasdaq as AAPL.

title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES

nodes.title: The Notes
key_items: The 2022 Notes; The 2024 Notes; The 0.000% 2025 Notes; The 0.875% 2025 Notes; The 2026 Notes
The 2027 Notes; The 1.375% 2029 Notes; The 3.050% 2029 Notes; The 2031 Notes; The 2042 Notes
nodes.summary: The text summarizes Apple’s euro- and sterling-denominated Notes, subject to the 2013 and 2018 Indentures with Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company as trustee. New York law governs; the Indentures impose no issuance limit and allow additional similar securities without holder consent, generally in the same series, subject to separate-ISIN rules. It lists each Notes series’ issue amount and date, maturity, annual or semiannual coupon and payment dates, and outstanding principal as of October 14, 2022: euro Notes maturing in 2022, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027, 2029 and 2031, and sterling Notes maturing in 2029 and 2042.

nodes.title: Ranking
nodes.summary: The Notes rank equally with the issuer’s other senior unsecured, unsubordinated debt, but are structurally subordinated to subsidiary debt and preferred stock and effectively subordinated to secured debt up to the value of collateral. Subsidiary creditors, including trade creditors and preferred stockholders, generally have priority over Noteholders in subsidiary assets and earnings. The Indentures do not limit the issuer or its subsidiaries from incurring additional debt.

nodes.title: Payment on the Notes
nodes.summary: Payments on the listed euro-denominated Notes are payable in euros, but switch to U.S. dollars if euros become unavailable or cease qualifying for use; conversion uses the Federal Reserve rate or, absent one, the latest Wall Street Journal rate from no later than the second Business Day before payment. Such dollar payments are not defaults. Sterling-denominated 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes are payable in pounds sterling, or euros if the UK adopts the euro, with the same dollar fallback, conversion method, and no-default protection. Business Day definitions specify relevant bank closures and, for euro Notes, TARGET2 availability.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: The Notes generally require principal and interest payments free of U.S. tax withholding unless legally required. The Company will pay non-U.S. holders additional amounts to preserve the stated net payment, subject to exceptions for holder connections or status, intermediaries and beneficial-owner eligibility, failures to provide required tax documentation, non-withholding taxes, late changes in law, specified non-income taxes, avoidable paying-agent withholding, late presentation, FATCA-related taxes, and combinations of these exceptions. The Notes remain subject to applicable tax laws, and the Company has no other tax-payment obligation. The text defines “United States” and “United States person” for these provisions and tax redemptions.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem an affected Notes series in whole, but not in part, if a post-prospectus-supplement U.S. tax-law change or change in official interpretation causes, or independent counsel concludes will cause, additional-amounts obligations. Redemption requires 30–60 days’ notice for the 2022, 2024, 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes; 15–60 days for the 0.875% 2025 and 1.375% 2029 Notes; or 10–60 days for the 0.000% 2025 and 2031 Notes. The price is 100% of principal plus accrued unpaid interest, excluding the redemption date for the latter two series.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption
nodes.summary: The terms permit optional redemption of specified notes at any time, in whole or part, using the greater of par or a discounted present-value amount based on remaining payments and a Comparable Government Bond Rate plus note-specific spreads. Four other note series may be redeemed before their stated Par Call Dates on similar make-whole terms; on or after those dates, redemption is at par. Accrued interest is paid through (but excluding) redemption, while interest due on or before that date is paid to holders of record. The text defines each series’ Par Call Date, the applicable German or UK Comparable Government Bond and selection process, and the yield-based method for calculating the Comparable Government Bond Rate.

nodes.title: Covenants
key_items: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The Indentures contain limited covenants and do not restrict the amount of debt or leases, debt secured by liens, or dividends, distributions, and purchases or redemptions of capital stock. They permit mergers, consolidations, and transfers of substantially all assets if the successor is appropriately organized in the U.S., assumes the obligations and conversion rights, and no default continues; under the 2013 Indenture, the trustee must also receive an officers’ certificate and counsel’s opinion. The successor replaces the issuer and assumes its rights and obligations, releasing the issuer. “Person” includes individuals, entities, governments, and their agencies or subdivisions.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: The Indentures define series-specific defaults: overdue interest (30 days), unpaid principal or premium, uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ notice (with 25% holder threshold under the 2013 Indenture and 33% under the 2018), specified voluntary or court-ordered bankruptcy events, and any additional series defaults. Bankruptcy definitions are provided. For continuing defaults, the trustee or qualifying holders may accelerate payment; bankruptcy-related defaults trigger automatic acceleration. A majority may rescind acceleration if specified sums are deposited and other defaults are cured or waived. Defaults need not affect other series. The issuer must provide the trustee an annual officer’s compliance/default statement within 120 days of fiscal year-end. Individual holders may bring proceedings only after notice, qualifying holder request, satisfactory trustee indemnity, trustee inaction for 60 days, and no contrary majority direction. A majority may direct remedies and waive certain defaults; the trustee’s duties and indemnity protections are described. Each holder retains an unconditional right to payment when due and to sue to enforce it.

nodes.title: Modification and Waivers
nodes.summary: The text explains amendment, waiver, and default rules under the Indentures. Amendments generally require majority approval by affected series holders, while changes to key payment, redemption, enforcement, voting, waiver, or conversion rights require each affected holder’s consent. It lists amendments the company and trustee may make without holder consent, including covenant, trustee, securities, administrative, and non-material changes. Series majorities may waive certain covenants and past defaults, except payment defaults and provisions requiring unanimous consent; a waiver cures only the specified default, not later or other defaults.

nodes.title: Discharge, Defeasance and Covenant Defeasance
nodes.summary: The text explains options to discharge near-term Notes by depositing sufficient funds, and legal or covenant defeasance through an irrevocable, adequately funded trust deposit. Covenant defeasance may leave the issuer liable for accelerated payments; eligible government obligations differ by note series (German or UK obligations for specified Notes). Tax opinions are required, with an IRS ruling or legal change needed for legal defeasance, which may follow covenant defeasance. Notes are book-entry globals held through Euroclear/Clearstream, but may become certificated under specified circumstances and denominations. It identifies BNYM as trustee and describes existing and potential banking and trustee relationships.

nodes.title: Note Defeasance, Settlement, Certificates and Trustee
nodes.summary: Defines eligible U.K. government obligations for defeasance of the 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes, and requires a tax opinion; legal defeasance may follow covenant defeasance. Notes are issued as global book-entry securities through Euroclear and Clearstream. They may be exchanged for definitive certificates in specified denominations if the depositary becomes unavailable without a successor within 90 days, the issuer elects to end global representation, or a continuing default occurs; otherwise global notes remain nonexchangeable except for replacement global notes. BNY Mellon Trust Company, N.A. is trustee and also has banking, custodial, trustee and paying-agent relationships with the issuer.

summary: Describes the euro- and sterling-denominated Notes, their terms, outstanding amounts, governing indentures, ranking, payment currencies and conversion rules, and additional-amounts and tax-redemption provisions. Covers optional make-whole and par redemptions; limited covenants and successor obligations; defaults, acceleration, holder remedies and trustee protections; amendments and waivers; discharge and defeasance requirements; global book-entry securities and circumstances for certificated Notes; and the trustee’s role and relationships.

title: Subsidiaries of Apple Inc.*
summary: Exhibit 21.1 lists Apple Inc. subsidiaries and their jurisdictions of incorporation: entities in Hong Kong, Delaware, Canada, China, Ireland, India, Arizona, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Australia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Nevada. A footnote states that other subsidiaries are omitted under Regulation S-K Item 601(b)(21)(ii) because, collectively, they were not significant subsidiaries at year-end. The text also begins Exhibit 23.1.

title: Consent of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
summary: Ernst & Young consents to incorporating its October 27, 2022 audit reports on Apple’s consolidated financial statements and internal control over financial reporting into eight specified Apple registration statements covering company securities, employee and director plans, deferred compensation, and Topsy Labs’ stock plan. CEO Timothy Cook and CFO Luca Maestri certify their review of Apple’s fiscal 2022 Form 10-K, the accuracy and fair presentation of its disclosures and financial information, and their responsibilities for disclosure and financial controls, including evaluation, reporting material changes, and notifying auditors and the audit committee of significant weaknesses or relevant fraud.

title: CERTIFICATIONS OF CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER AND CHIEF FINANCIAL OFFICER PURSUANT TO 18 U.S.C. SECTION 1350, AS ADOPTED PURSUANT TO SECTION 906 OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002
summary: Apple CEO Timothy D. Cook and CFO Luca Maestri certify under Section 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act that Apple’s FY2022 Form 10-K complies with relevant Securities Exchange Act requirements and fairly presents the company’s financial condition and operating results. Both signed on October 27, 2022. Apple retains the signed original and will provide it to the SEC upon request.
